prompt.context: Our client is a steel manufacturing company in the Netherlands. They are considering investing in an advanced analytics tool that will help them better predict inventory schedule. They are also looking at immediate methods to save costs.
prompt.question: A) Steel coils are currently transported from the factory to customers via Railways, Trucks, Vessels and Barges. Analyze these four transport methods and suggest any opportunities for cost saving. B) Suggest any alternative techniques to save cost in the immediate future.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company operate domestically or internationally?

clarifying_info.a: Predominantly large B2B manufacturers with both short-term and long-term contracts.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the company manufacture?
clarifying_info.a: For this case, assume steel is only manufactured as coils.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific cost-saving target?
clarifying_info.a: No specific target; the objective is simply to identify cost-saving opportunities.

exhibits.title: Transport Method Data
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four transport methods — Rail, Truck, Barge, and Vessel — across five metrics.

exhibits.title: Pier-to-Truck Transfer Volume Over 21 Weeks
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of steel coils transferred from the pier to trucks each week over a 21-week period. Total volume for delivery is 5,700 steel coils; 1 steel coil = 10 tons. A spike is visible in weeks 1–2.

data.spike: Weeks 1–2 show the highest transfer volumes (approximately 1,500–2,000 coils each), suggesting overflow from vessels onto trucks.

framework: Focus on costs as the primary driver; cover profitability briefly for context
Incorporate steel industry specifics: heavy/bulk goods, long-haul international logistics, coil-specific handling
Evaluate all four transport modes (Rail, Truck, Barge, Vessel) on capacity utilization and cost/ton
Calculate weekly cost and cost-saving potential per mode by improving utilization to 100%
Cross-reference transport modes to identify operational mismatches (e.g., vessel overflow to truck)
Address Part B: alternative / immediate cost-saving levers beyond transport optimization
Synthesize into a prioritized recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the weekly cost for each transport mode and the cost-saving potential if utilization is optimized to 100%.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply Deliveries/Week × Volume/Delivery to get Volume/Week, then multiply by Cost/ton for weekly cost. Cost saving = weekly cost × (1 – utilization). Vessel has 100% utilization so no saving. Rail has the largest absolute saving.

math.setup: Volume/week = Deliveries/week × Volume/delivery; Cost/week = Volume/week × Cost/ton; Saving = Cost/week × (100% − Utilization%)
math.answer: $7.3M total weekly cost-saving potential through full capacity utilization across Rail, Truck, and Barge

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows coils being transferred from the pier to trucks over 21 weeks. Why is this happening, and what is the cost of this inefficiency?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cross-reference Exhibit 1: vessels load every 14 days and run at 100% utilization. Overflow coils left behind on the pier must be trucked instead of shipped by vessel. The cheaper vessel rate is $10/ton vs. $30/ton for truck. Weeks 1–2 show ~3,000 coils stranded. Weeks 3–21 (2,700 coils) represent avoidable truck usage with better inventory management. An excellent candidate also notes that the 100% KPI on vessels forces them to leave coils behind; reducing the KPI target to 95% would allow a buffer.

math.setup: Avoidable truck coils = total coils − coils in weeks 1–2 (unavoidable); saving = avoidable coils × weight per coil × (truck cost − vessel cost)
steps: Total coils = 5,700; coils in weeks 1–2 (unavoidable) = ~3,000; avoidable coils = 5,700 − 3,000 = 2,700
math.answer: $540,000 saving by avoiding unnecessary pier-to-truck transfers through better inventory management

brainstorming.prompt: What other immediate cost-saving techniques could the client pursue beyond transport optimization?

categories.name: Procurement & Input Costs
ideas: Renegotiate raw material contracts leveraging scale
Consolidate supplier base for volume discounts
Explore alternative steel inputs or alloys if spec allows

categories.name: Production & Operations
ideas: Optimize furnace / rolling mill scheduling to reduce energy peaks
Reduce scrap/waste rates through tighter process controls
Preventive maintenance to avoid costly unplanned downtime
Cross-train workers to reduce idle labor during demand troughs

categories.name: Inventory Management
ideas: Implement demand forecasting (tie back to the analytics tool investment)
Reduce safety stock by tightening supply-demand alignment
Move toward just-in-time delivery for key B2B customers

categories.name: Transport & Logistics (additional)
ideas: Renegotiate cost/ton rates with carriers given volume
Shift marginal truck volume to rail or barge where geography allows
Explore backhaul agreements to monetize empty return capacity
Consolidate small shipments to reduce frequency and improve load factor

categories.name: Customer & Contract
ideas: Revisit delivery frequency in long-term contracts — less frequent deliveries improve utilization
Offer customers incentives to accept consolidated shipments
Introduce surcharges for rush or small-lot deliveries to reflect true cost

recommendation: Pursue ~$7.84M in total cost savings: $7.3M from improving capacity utilization on Rail, Truck, and Barge, and $540K from better inventory management to eliminate pier-to-truck overflow on vessel deliveries
Continue investing in the advanced analytics tool, as improved demand forecasting directly addresses the inventory mismatch identified as a key cost driver
risks: Assumptions about average utilization rates may not hold — actual utilization may vary by route or season
Truck drivers may be unionized; reducing the number of active trucks could require renegotiating labor contracts
Changing vessel KPIs from 100% to 95% may face internal resistance and require change-management effort
next_steps: Modify vessel labor KPIs to target 95% utilization instead of 100% to create a buffer and reduce pier overflow
Gradually reduce the number of active trucks as utilization improves, shifting volume to lower-cost Rail and Barge
Renegotiate cost/ton rates with carriers where volume leverage exists
Accelerate implementation of the advanced analytics tool to embed demand forecasting into scheduling
